title: Recurrent and predictable species assemblages in a pelagic longline fishery
content:
Abstract
Pelagic longline fisheries interact with diverse bycatch communities, yet management is typically framed at the level of individual species rather than multispecies catch structure. Here, I evaluate whether predictable bycatch assemblages in the Hawaiʻi pelagic longline fishery are also selectively avoidable. Using observer data from 117 789 fishing sets (1994–2025), I identified recurrent assemblages separately for shallow-set (swordfish-directed) and deep-set (tuna-directed) sectors using a distance-based clustering framework applied to proportional catch composition, and assessed whether dominant ecological structure was preserved across alternative representations of the data. Three shallow-set assemblages were identified, including a Swordfish Dominant assemblage, a Blue Shark Dominant assemblage, and an epipelagic assemblage with reduced shark representation, whereas deep sets resolved into two more weakly separated assemblages reflecting variation within a shared pelagic predator community. Although exact set-level assignments varied among data treatments, the underlying ecological gradients, particularly contrasts between shark-rich and shark-poor operational states (sets with relatively high versus low shark catch), remained consistent. Forecasting analyses focused on the Blue Shark Dominant assemblage, which was moderately predictable (mean AUC ≈ 0.76) using season and location. Scenario-based analyses showed that avoiding this assemblage could reduce blue shark catch substantially while disproportionately sparing swordfish catch, with this selectivity advantage greatest at modest reduction targets, whereas in deep sets avoidance of shark-rich conditions resulted in nearly proportional losses of target tuna catch. These contrasting outcomes demonstrate that predictability alone does not guarantee selective mitigation. Instead, assemblage structure determines whether bycatch risk can be decoupled from target catch or reflects fundamental ecological coupling. Assemblage-based forecasting therefore provides a diagnostic framework for identifying when dynamic avoidance is feasible and when management must instead address unavoidable trade-offs.
